extracted.intended_audience: academic press officers, researchers, and science journalists
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for writing accurate academic press releases about health/biomedical research, focused on avoiding exaggeration and increasing accountability and transparency. Includes specific types of exaggeration to avoid plus recommended structural and procedural practices for press releases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid exaggeration in academic press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases should avoid making claims that go beyond those made in the peer-reviewed research paper; improving the accuracy of academic press releases could reduce misleading health-related news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors conclude that 'most of the inflation detected ... was already present in the text of the press releases produced by academics and their establishments,' so press releases are a primary target for improving accuracy and reducing misleading news.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not give direct behavioural advice beyond the paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'giving direct advice to readers to change their behaviour' unless the underlying study and paper explicitly justify such advice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study identified 'giving direct advice to readers to change their behaviour' as a common type of exaggeration; 40% of press releases examined contained exaggerated advice compared with the corresponding peer-reviewed articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not make causal claims from correlational data
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid turning correlational (observational) findings into causal claims in the press release when the original study does not support causation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study flagged 'making causal claims from correlational (observational) data' as a frequent exaggeration; 33% of press releases contained exaggerated causal claims. When press releases contained causal exaggeration, news uptake of causal language was much higher (81%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not infer human relevance from animal findings
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid asserting or implying that animal study results directly apply to humans when the paper does not support such inferences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The study identified 'making inference about humans from animal findings' as a common exaggeration; 36% of press releases contained such exaggeration, and when present the news often repeated it (86%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include named individuals from the original research paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Press releases should 'include named individuals from the original research paper' to increase traceability and accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ben Goldacre suggests that naming researchers connects press releases to the scholarly record and supports accountability for any exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link the press release to the promoted peer-reviewed paper
rubrics_metrics.description: Every press release should be explicitly linked to the peer-reviewed paper it is promoting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goldacre argues press releases 'should be linked to the paper they are promoting' so readers and peers can verify claims and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present press releases as online data appendices, visible to peers
rubrics_metrics.description: Make press releases available as online data appendices associated with the publication and in full view of peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Presenting press releases as appendices would 'produce an information trail, and accountability among peers and the public.' This increases transparency and allows peer scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide opportunity for feedback in the publishing journal
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should enable feedback mechanisms for press releases associated with published papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goldacre suggests 'there should also be opportunity for feedback in the publishing journal' so the academic community can comment on or correct exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat academic press releases as part of the scientific publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider press releases a component of the scientific publication process, subject to the same accountability and transparency expectations as other publication elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing press releases as part of the publication creates an 'information trail' and holds authors and institutions accountable for claims made in press materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid institutional self-promotion and sensational language
rubrics_metrics.description: Press offices and researchers should avoid language rooted in 'university competition and self promotion' and resist sensationalising findings for publicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors note the blame for exaggeration 'lies mainly with the increasing culture of university competition and self promotion, interacting with the increasing pressures on journalists to do more with less time.' Reducing self-promotional framing can limit inflation of claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider public ranking or accountability mechanisms for press releases
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementing public rankings or other accountability systems for press releases might change academic behaviour and reduce routine misleading of patients and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Goldacre speculates that a 'public ranking of press releases might change academic behaviour' by creating reputational incentives to avoid exaggeration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise that press-release exaggeration propagates into news
rubrics_metrics.description: Because exaggeration present in press releases strongly predicts exaggeration in subsequent news stories, minimizing press-release exaggeration is crucial to prevent misleading media coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical findings: when press releases contained exaggeration, news exaggeration rates were much higher (e.g., 58% for advice, 81% for causal claims, 86% for inference to humans); when press releases did not contain exaggeration, news exaggeration rates were low (17%, 18%, 10%, respectively).
